Domain Review
There are 25 Domains Across 4 Authority Tiers. 
1. The Data Spine (purple) sits at the top. ProgramGroupYears is the universal FK chain
everything else hangs off. 
2. Tier 1 (black) holds the four domains that decide money, eligibility, and enforcement —
nothing else in the system makes those calls. 
3. Tier 2 (grey) constrains inputs but never decides outcomes. 
4. Tier 3 (blue) owns program-specific rules and operational modules. 
5. Tier 4 (green) consumes facts but never influences behavior. 
387 tables live in one shared cnp_global database; 1,015 tables live in a separate cnp_ops
database per state. The database itself is the tenant boundary so no TenantId column is
needed.

The Problems We're Solving
Reading the legacy CTS and DIS repositories revealed five patterns that define why the current
system can't scale:
The same logic forks by state.
Missouri's federal report BLL is already 50% larger than Utah's — same form, same federal
requirement, different file because state-specific logic migrated into code instead of
configuration. Every state added makes the next one harder to maintain.
Business rules exist but don't run
The CACFP Institution Management Plan has over 80 compliance rules fully coded. The entire
validation method is commented out. Only one field is checked at submission. States have been
operating without that enforcement for years — not because the rules don't matter, but because
they were never turned on.
Schema versions live in application code
Hawaii's DC application tracks which database schema version it's talking to using hardcoded
year constants that branch SQL queries. Three schema versions co-exist in production today.
The code — not migrations, not the database — is managing the difference.
State-specific data is embedded in source code
SFTP IP addresses, plaintext credentials, and PGP key file paths are string literals and
app.config values. There was no configuration system to put them in, so they went into code.
Every state deployment made that worse.
Business logic is in the database and diverging
SQL CLR functions handle name matching. Custom sequence generators manage key
allocation. Stored procedures encode logic that runs outside application visibility. The database
has become a second application layer — one that's harder to test, harder to version, and harder
to move.
4 · Observational
Reporting & Analytics (→ Snowflake)  ·  Audit & Observability  ·  Notifications  ·  Reference Data &
Transparency  ·  LaunchDarkly

What We Need to Finish It
The design was built from what I could read. I couldnʼt access some of the most important
logic.
Several stored procedures were encrypted (deliberately, and correctly) to protect LINQ's
intellectual property after incidents where states attempted to modify or redistribute our
software. That was the right call. The consequence is that the offshore team cannot
characterize or reimplement what those procedures do without seeing them first.
Before those modules can be assigned to a sprint, we need two things:
1. Decrypted procedure source so the logic can be characterized and tested before migration
(cloud ops?)
2. Engineer knowledge from this team the people who built those procedures, who know the
edge cases, who remember why a particular branch exists.
The offshore team can build from design documents. They cannot build from institutional
memory they don't have access to. The internal team's involvement in characterizing this logic is
the only way it can come together  correctly.

DESIGN DECISIONS
1. Eligibility snapshot is frozen at approval: The eligibility snapshot (enrollment counts, rate tier
qualifications, site program configuration) is captured from the approved application and
never modified. Dollar rates are not stored in ClaimLaws, they are resolved at claim calculation
time from ClaimRateAmounts using the claim date as the effective date key. Immutable record
of what was decided about eligibility, not about rates.
2. ProgramGroupYears is the data spine: Every entity FKs through ProgramGroupYears. It is
the universal join key across all domains.
3. Database IS the tenant boundary: No TenantId column in cnp_ops. Schema name = state =
tenant. Clean isolation by design.
4. JSONB for rules and configuration: Rules, overrides, and configuration stored as JSONB —
eliminates schema forking for state-specific logic.
5. Federal SPs to PostgreSQL functions: Characterization tests required before any translation.
Stored procedures encode business logic that may be undocumented.

Data Spine
Every piece of data in this platform has to answer two questions: 
1. which federal program is this for
2. which school year does it cover? 
This section is the single source of truth for both. When USDA publishes a new school year
starting October 1, this is where that year is registered. Everything else in the system links back
here so those two questions always have a consistent, reliable answer.
The data spine immediately communicates what ProgramGroups → ProgramGroupYears →
ProgramGroupEnrollments does: every Application and every Claim FK-chains through
ProgramGroupYears. Without this chain we cannot build a correctly joined data model.

THE PROBLEMS THIS DATA SPINE SOLVES
This implementation solves 4 problems:
1. Join consistency breaks.  If Claims stores programCode = 'NSLP'  and Applications
stores programCode = 'SNP'  and some legacy table stores programCode = '9' , we
cannot reliably join them. ProgramGroupYears is a stable integer FK so joins are always exact.
2. Year boundary logic becomes application code. With loose strings, every query that spans a
year boundary has to know that NSLP SY2025-26 started Oct 1, 2025. With
ProgramGroupYears, that knowledge is in the database: WHERE pgyr.StartDate <=
@claimDate AND pgyr.EndDate >= @claimDate .
3. Rate changes add risk. If Claims stores the rate directly, a rate correction in July affects
every past claim that gets reprocessed. The spine separates the rate lookup table
(ClaimRateAmounts , effective-dated) from the frozen eligibility snapshot applied to a
specific claim (ClaimLaws ).. The spine makes this separation structurally enforceable.
4. Multi-program sponsors are hard to query. A sponsor like Salt Lake City SD participates in
NSLP, CACFP, and SFSP. If program is a string field on the sponsor record, we end up with
ProgramGroupYear → ProgramMealRates
→ knows which grant account to deduct
from
7. When the FNSReport is generated, it
aggregates all Claims for 
ProgramGroupYearId = NSLP
SY2025-26  for this tenant

ClaimLaws — never the live rate table.
Every step in that chain joins through ProgramGroupYears.

Tier 1
CLAIMS & REIMBURSMENT
85 tables  ·  Tier 1 Authoritative  ·  Money and Enforcement
When a school district submits their monthly report of how many free, reduced, and paid meals
they served, that report lives here. The system checks it against the rules that were locked in
when the district applied. If something doesn't add up, the error is flagged here and the
payment is held until it's resolved.
Claims is the parent record. When a sponsor submits a monthly claim, one Claims row is
created. ClaimDetails has one row per site per claim containing the actual meal counts
(Free/Reduced/Paid) plus NonCongregateTtl for non-congregate modes. ClaimLaws ClaimLaws
is the most architecturally significant entity on the slide. It stores the eligibility snapshot
extracted from the approved application at the time of approval — enrollment counts, rate tier
qualifications (Severe Need eligibility, CEP ISP percentage, performance-based eligibility), and
site program configuration. It does not store dollar rates. Dollar rates are looked up from
ClaimRateAmounts at claim calculation time using the claim date as the effective date key. The
two mechanisms work together: ClaimLaws prevents application changes from retroactively
altering a sponsor's tier qualifications on already-processed claims; ClaimRateAmounts
effective-dating ensures a revised prior-year claim always resolves to the rate in effect on its
original claim date, not the current year's rate.. ClaimErrors tracks every validation failure with a
BrokenInd flag — when all errors are resolved, the claim can proceed. AcceptClaims and 
AcceptClaimSessions handle the batch acceptance workflow where state agencies lock and
approve groups of claims together. Adjustments handles post-approval corrections.

ACCOUNTING & FINANCE
147 tables  ·  Tier 1 Authoritative  · financial instruments
When a state agency is ready to pay a school district for their approved meals, the payment
runs through here. The federal grant that funds the payment is tracked here. If a school district
was overpaid and owes money back, the repayment plan lives here. Every dollar that enters or
leaves the program on the state agency's side is recorded here.
This is the financial chain: Grants fund Disbursements; FNSReports aggregate the activity;
RepaymentSchedules track money owed back; and AnnualFinancialReport (Indiana + Maine
reference implementation) tracks independent financial audits.

ELIGIBILITY & DIRECT CERTIFICATION
147 tables  ·  Tier 1 Authoritative  · eligibility determination
Before a child can receive a free or reduced-price meal, someone has to establish that they
qualify. For many children, that determination happens automatically: the state matches school
enrollment records against food assistance databases like SNAP and Medicaid overnight. If the
system finds a match, the child is certified without anyone filling out a paper form. This section
is where that matching process runs, where uncertain matches wait for a human to confirm
them, and where the final list of eligible students is kept.
This is a dual-layer DC model: Core2_DirectCertificationMatches (the modern 98-table layer
present in CO/IA/OH/WY but absent from Georgia) sitting alongside FreeRedcStudentEligibility
(the legacy dbo layer). DirectVer Session is Indiana's unique contribution, the only DIS state that
lets sponsors resolve possible DC matches themselves rather than waiting for state agency
intervention. OctoberSurveyForms captures the annual building-level enrollment data used for
verification sample sizes.

against the student roster for Utah DOE.

"Maria Chen, DOB 2017-04-12, 437 South

COMPLIANCE & ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW
~375 tables  ·  Tier 1 Authoritative  ·  enforcement and fiscal accountability
When a state agency visits a school to check whether meals are being served correctly, every
piece of evidence they collect is recorded here. If they find the school overclaimed meals, the
financial penalty is calculated here too. If the situation is serious enough to remove a sponsor
from the program entirely, that legal record lives in its own protected space.
The mental model of compliance review is simple: reviewer visits sponsor, records pass/fail,
done. The reality is much more complex. The USDA requires state agencies to collect extremely
specific evidence for each type of finding, and each finding type has its own data structure. A
meal observation form for a CACFP center has different fields than a meal observation form for
a DCH provider. A five-day food production reconciliation has different fields than a milk audit.
Each of those requires its own detail table, its own error table, its own status table, and its own
summary table. Multiply that across all program types and all finding categories and 375 tables
is where you land.
Example

Serious Deficiency
<!-- page: 24 -->
SeriousDeficiency  lives in a separate [serdef]  schema for regulatory reasons. When
USDA's regulations require a state agency to initiate serious deficiency proceedings, the
documentation of that proceeding must be legally defensible in an appeal. Placing it in a
separate schema creates a clear audit boundary. No other domain's queries can accidentally
modify SerDef records. The schema isolationsupports the regulatory requirement that SerDef
records be immutable once issued.
The SerDef data model includes:
SeriousDeficiency  the core record
SeriousDeficiencyTriggers  what finding triggered the proceeding (there are specific
regulatory categories that mandate a SerDef)
SeriousDeficiencyUnits  which of the sponsor's sites or homes are implicated 
SeriousDeficiencyAppealTypes  the sponsor's options for contesting
TerminationEvents  If the proceeding results in termination from the program
A SerDef that's resolved without termination is closed; one that results in termination is
permanently recorded in TerminationEvents  and affects whether the sponsor can reapply
in the future.

Risk scoring and how it feeds the 3-year cycle
RiskScores  is not a single computed number. It's a multi-factor calculation that the system
runs periodically for every sponsor. The inputs typically include: 
time since last review
any open findings from prior reviews
claim error rate over the past year
poverty level of the service area
any compliance history with FNA
whether the sponsor has been flagged by another agency. 
The output is a risk level (Low / Medium / High) and a computed score. High-risk sponsors are
reviewed annually rather than once every three years.
ReviewCycles  (in the Reviews domain) is driven by RiskScores . The risk score determines
both the frequency of review and the prioritization within the review queue. State agencies with
limited reviewer capacity use risk scores to decide which sponsors get reviewed this year
versus next year. Without risk scoring, a state agency would either review sponsors randomly or
in alphabetical order, both of which miss the sponsors most likely to have problems.
Procurement Review (FSMC)
ProcurementReviews  is a compliance track that applies to all sponsors under 2 CFR 200 and
7 CFR 210.21 — not just those using a Food Service Management Company. FSMC is an
additional conditional layer on top of the baseline, not the gate for the review itself. All sponsors
are subject to the general procurement section:
Competitive bidding processes, solicitation methods, small purchase thresholds, and general
procurement compliance under 2 CFR 200 FSMC sponsors only are subject to additional
sections: 
Contract management, management fee reconciliation, USDA Foods pass-through, fee caps
(sponsor-level) 
FSMC contract amendments, USDA Foods management at the site level, contract
performance (site-level) 
A procurement review examines whether the sponsor followed required procurement
procedures. For FSMC sponsors, it also examines the FSMC contract terms and compliance.
The data model for procurement review includes: 
<!-- page: 29 -->
AdminReviewProcurementAuthority  who authorized the procurement decision 
AdminReviewProcurementCodes  the specific regulatory requirements being examined
AdminReviewProcurementVendors  the vendors who bid and the selection rationale 
AdminReviewProcurementSmallPurchase  and 
AdminReviewProcurementGroupPurchase different procurement methods that have
different requirements (apply to all sponsors)
AdminReviewProcurementCashInLieu  for SFSP sponsors who provide cash instead of
commodities
Procurement review can happen during a regular administrative review or as a standalone
review triggered by a complaint or by the sponsor entering into a new FSMC contract. This is
why ProcurementReviews  has a FK to AdminReviewId  that can be null. A standalone
procurement review exists without a parent administrative review.
Fiscal actions moved to Compliance in this model. A fiscal action is the consequence of a review
finding of overclaiming. It doesn't represent money the state agency is owed in the same way a
grant disbursement represents money the state agency owes a sponsor. It represents the
quantified consequence of an enforcement action. The repayment schedule that flows from a
fiscal action, and the actual recovery of funds, belongs in Accounting because that's the
financial instrument. But the calculation of how much is owed, and the legal record of why,
belongs in Compliance where the review lives.
If fiscal actions live in Accounting, we create a circular dependency: the Accounting domain
needs to know about Review findings to generate fiscal actions, which means Accounting needs
to read from Compliance. With fiscal actions in Compliance, Accounting only needs to receive
the final assessed amount and create a Repayment Schedule against it. The domain boundary is
clean.

Tier 2 | Core Supporting Domains
Operational backbone: sponsors, applications, access, and configuration
Sponsor & Site Registry
Every organization that participates in the program (school districts, daycare centers, summer
camps) is registered here. Every location where meals are actually served is registered here too.
This is the authoritative list of who is in the program and where they operate. When a new
organization wants to join, they start here. When a site closes, that change is recorded here.
This holds the master records of who participates. Sites now carry Latitude and Longitude,
generalizing the Missouri ArcGIS pattern to all states rather than keeping it Missouri-only.
Applications & Agreements
Every year, each participating organization has to renew their agreement to follow program
rules. That renewal process, including the forms, the attachments, the approval workflow, lives
here. Before a new organization can participate, they go through a pre-screening process that's
also tracked here. The forms change slightly each year, and this section keeps track of which
version of each form was in effect when an organization applied.
This the largest Tier 2 domain at ~173 tables, covering the full application lifecycle including
PotentialSponsor (a DIS capability brought forward that tracks prospects before formal
application), the AnnualForms generalized framework, FSMC contracts, and VCA Checklists.

Identity & Access
Every person who logs into the system is governed by what's stored here. A state agency
reviewer can see all sponsors in their state; a school district employee sees only their own
district's data. These boundaries are enforced at the service layer on every request.
This section contains the RBAC tables that replaced the legacy CnpObjects ACL. Rather than
5,082 individual permission rows, the new model uses approximately 180 named permissions
organized into roles. Per-state variation is handled through TenantRoleOverrides  rather
than separate permission definitions per state. The core tables are: PermissionCatalog , 
Roles , RolePermissions , TenantRoleOverrides , UserRoleAssignments , and 
SponsorUserAccess . Full design in .
Configuration & Tenant
USDA publishes new reimbursement rates every July. Rather than requiring a software update
every year, those rates are stored in ClaimRateAmounts  with an effective date. When July 1
arrives, the new rates are available for claim calculation. Applications approved after July 1 will
have a ClaimLaws eligibility snapshot that captures the new school year's tier qualifications.
Claims resolve dollar rates from ClaimRateAmounts  using the claim date as the effective date
key.  Prior-year claims always return prior-year rates regardless of when they are revised or
reprocessed. State-specific settings that don't involve federal rules (workflow preferences,
notification templates, local thresholds) live here too.
ClaimRateAmounts  sits between meals served and the federal funding available to pay for
them. Given a ProgramCode , MealType , and EligibilityCategory , it returns the
reimbursement rate the federal government applies to that meal. Annual rate updates are
INSERT statements here, not code deployments. Lives in cnp_global  — no tenant scope,
because federal rates are the same across all states.

Tier 3 
PROGRAM DOMAINS (SNP, CACFP, DCH, SFSP, SSFO)
Specialist domains, each with its own application/claim/compliance stack
Program Domains (SNP, CACFP, DCH, SFSP, SSFO) represent one federal program with its
own application/claim/compliance stack. 
School Nutrition Programs (SNP)
The National School Lunch Program is the flagship program that feeds the most children in the
most schools every day. This section covers the rules, forms, and calculations specific to school
meal programs: which schools qualify for enhanced funding, how summer meal service works,
how meal pattern compliance is tracked, and how schools that serve all students for free under
the Community Eligibility Provision calculate their reimbursement.
It includes OctoberSurveyForms  and ProvisionRatios (Provision 2 and 3 provisional percentage
tables). 
Child & Adult Care Food Program (CACFP)
Daycare centers, after-school programs, and adult care facilities operate under a different set of
rules than K-12 schools. Children in these settings eat different meal patterns at different times,
and the providers serving them range from large nonprofit institutions to individual home-based
providers. This section covers the forms, claims, and compliance requirements for all of them,
including the annual self-assessment that every sponsoring organization must complete to
demonstrate they're capable of running the program.

This includes VCAChecklists, the 16-table self-assessment that gates application approval. 
Day Care Home (DCH)
Home-based childcare providers — someone running a licensed daycare out of their own house
— are treated differently from institutional daycare centers. They participate through a
sponsoring organization that monitors them, and they're reimbursed at rates that depend on
whether the provider and neighborhood meet low-income thresholds. This section tracks every
home-based provider, their applications, their monthly meal claims, and which reimbursement
tier they fall into.
This is a distinct provider-based model where individual home-based providers claim meals
under a sponsoring organization. It does not share the site model used by CACFP centers. 
Summer Food Service Program (SFSP)
When school is out and cafeterias are closed, children in lower-income communities lose
access to the free meals they depend on during the school year. The Summer Food Service
Program fills that gap by funding meals at summer camps, parks, libraries, and community
centers. This section covers the sites that serve summer meals, how sites can distribute meals
as pickup or grab-and-go when children can't gather in one place, and how those summer
operations are funded and monitored.
This includes NonCongregateRequest with the three-mode enforcement model (congregate
only, non-congregate only, mixed). 
Seamless Summer Food Option (SSFO)
Some schools that already operate the National School Lunch Program want to continue serving
meals through the summer without switching to different rules and paperwork. The Seamless
Summer Food Option lets them use school-year administrative procedures but summer funding.
This section tracks those schools separately from SFSP so that the two programs' different rules
don't get mixed together.
SSFO was added as a first-class program domain based on the architect's recommendation; it
has ~16 dedicated tables with distinct ClaimLaws from NSLP, preventing SSFO quirks from
bleeding into NSLP claim validation.
Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Program (FFVP)
A USDA grant that gives selected elementary schools a dollar allocation to purchase and serve
fresh fruits and vegetables as snacks during the school day. It is not a meal reimbursement
program — there's no per-meal rate and no ClaimLaws. Schools apply for a per-student budget
allocation, spend it on produce, and report expenditures back to the state.
<!-- page: 34 -->
The financial instrument is completely different from every other program. Instead of "meals
served × reimbursement rate = payment," the model is "approved allocation → expenditure
tracking → unexpended balance." A school doesn't submit a monthly meal count claim; they
submit an expenditure report showing what they spent on produce.FFVPSiteInvitations
Community Eligibility Provision (CEP)
An election within NSLP/SBP that lets high-poverty schools serve all students free meals
without collecting individual household income applications. A school qualifies if its Identified
Student Percentage (ISP) — the ratio of directly-certified students to total enrollment — is 40%
or higher. Once elected, the school is reimbursed at a blended rate: (ISP × 1.6) × free meal rate
+ remainder × paid meal rate. The multiplier of 1.6 is set by federal regulation and cannot be
configured.
Changes how reimbursement is calculated for SNP/NSLPclaims. The ISP calculation, the group
management (schools can pool together to hit the 40% threshold), and the annual election
process all have their own data structures that would clutter the SNP tables if embedded there.

SPECIALIST MODULES
VCA Checklist Before a childcare sponsoring organization can participate in CACFP, it has to
demonstrate it's actually capable of running the program responsibly: financially solvent,
operationally capable, and accountable for the homes or centers under its umbrella. That annual
self-assessment, scored against a standard federal rubric, is what lives here. A sponsor that
scores below the passing threshold cannot have its application approved until the gaps are
addressed.
Budget Module Some program types require sponsors to submit a detailed budget alongside
their application by projecting their food costs, labor costs, and administrative expenses for the
year. This section stores those budget submissions, the line-item breakdowns, and the approval
status. It's the financial accountability layer that lets state agencies verify a sponsor is planning
to spend program funds appropriately before approving their participation.
Waivers & Approvals Sometimes a sponsor needs to do something the standard rules don't
permit. Each exception requires written approval from the state agency or USDA before it
happens. This section tracks those requests, the approvals, and the outcomes — so there's a
clear record that exceptions were properly authorized.
Without this domain, exceptions disappear into email inboxes. A USDA auditor asking "was this
sole-source contract approved before the sponsor signed it?" should have a single place to go
for the answer, not a search through three years of email.

LaunchDarkly
Every month, every state agency submits federal reports to USDA proving that program funds
were spent correctly, that the right number of children were served, and that reimbursements
match what was claimed. Generating those reports from a live operational database would mean
running complex multi-year aggregations against the same tables that state agency staff use to
approve claims in real time — a query that takes 45 seconds to build a federal summary would
block a claim approval for 45 seconds. This domain solves that by maintaining a separate read-
optimized copy of all operational data in Snowflake. The operational database records
transactions; Snowflake answers questions about them. Nothing in this domain writes back to
any other domain. It consumes facts; it never influences behavior. 
Tier 4 is  a different read/write contract: it only reads. The consequence of this separation is that
the reporting infrastructure can be rebuilt, reconfigured, or replaced without touching a single
table in the operational database. The operational system doesn't know Snowflake exists. The
reporting system doesn't need to know how a claim was approved, it only needs the final
approved state.
This is also why federal report restatements are safe. When a state needs to resubmit a
corrected FNS-777 for a prior year, the Snowflake copy reflects the current state of the
operational database including any post-approval adjustments. FNSReportLineItems stores
what was submitted previously so the delta is auditable. The operational ClaimLaws records are
untouched.
Documents & AttachmentsEvery form submission, every approval, and every review generates
documents — PDFs, spreadsheets, uploaded certificates. This section stores them. It also
generates a snapshot — a frozen PDF of exactly what a form looked like at the moment it was
submitted or approved — so that months later, anyone can see not just the current state of a
record but what it looked like at every significant point in its lifecycle.
128 tables embedded in shared dbo schema. Cannot be cleanly separated without
schema surgery. Migration planning is blocked until scope is decided.
<!-- page: 38 -->
Communications & Emails State agencies communicate with sponsors regularly — deadline
reminders, approval notices, requests for additional information. The templates for those
communications live here, along with the record of what was sent, to whom, and when. Some
states maintain email distribution lists for bulk outreach to all sponsors of a particular program
type; that capability lives here too."
FTP & IntegrationThe platform exchanges data with outside systems — state benefit agencies
for Direct Certification, USDA for commodity orders, state financial systems for payment
processing. The configuration for those data connections, the log of files transferred, and the
record of what succeeded and what failed all live here. Several of these integrations exist today
as separate applications in the LINQ codebase; those applications are architecturally sound but
have not received recent maintenance and will need to be rebuilt, not simply migrated."
Workflow & TasksCertain processes in the platform happen automatically in the background —
the nightly job that checks for new benefit matches, the annual job that rolls every application
forward into a new program year at midnight on October 1, the scheduled alerts that fire when a
claim has been sitting unreviewed too long. This section manages the scheduling and execution
of those background jobs, the task lists assigned to state agency staff, and the calendar of
review deadlines.
Reporting & AnalyticsEvery FNS report submitted to USDA — the monthly participation data,
the financial status report, the annual program summary — is generated from here. Unlike the
operational database, which is optimized for recording transactions, this section reads from a
separate analytics warehouse (Snowflake) that is optimized for summarizing large amounts of
historical data. Reports run against Snowflake instead of the main database so that generating a
complex federal report never slows down a state agency employee trying to approve a claim.

Audit & Observability
~18 tables · Tier 4 Observational · append-only audit infrastructure
Every action a user takes, every field they change, and every status transition a record passes
through is captured here. This domain never influences program behavior — no claim decision,
no compliance outcome, and no eligibility determination reads from it. It exists entirely to
answer questions after the fact: what happened, who did it, when, and what did the record look
like at each moment in its lifecycle.
The domain addresses the compliance requirement from the WIP CNP Platform Replacement
spec: historical compliance states must be queryable at any point in time without manual
reconstruction. A USDA auditor examining a review from two years ago should be able to ask
the system "what did this application look like at the moment of approval?" and receive a
structured, query-ready answer — not be handed a PDF to read manually.
The domain has three tables with distinct but complementary responsibilities. AuditLogs
captures who touched what and when — a lightweight record of every action. EntitySnapshots
captures a full structured snapshot of a record's key fields at each status transition — the
machine-queryable version of what FormSnapshot captures as a PDF. FieldChangeLog captures
every individual field edit, including changes that happen between status transitions and would
otherwise be invisible to the snapshot record.
Relationship to FormSnapshot
FormSnapshot (in Documents & Attachments) and EntitySnapshots are triggered by the same
event — a status change — but serve different audiences. FormSnapshot renders a PDF to S3
for human review and legal defensibility. EntitySnapshots stores JSONB to the database for
machine queries and report generation. An auditor opening a case file uses FormSnapshot. The
<!-- page: 42 -->
system generating a compliance summary report uses EntitySnapshots. Both are needed;
neither replaces the other.
How the three audit tables work together
Together these three tables satisfy all five audit requirements from the WIP spec without event
sourcing: 100% user action capture, 100% data change capture, 100% workflow transition
capture, point-in-time compliance queryability, and no 
All three tables are append-only
No row in AuditLogs, EntitySnapshots, or FieldChangeLog is ever updated or deleted in normal
operation. The audit trail is only meaningful if it cannot be altered after the fact. Deletion of audit
records requires a separate privileged data retention process outside normal application code,
triggered only for regulatory compliance (e.g., GDPR deletion requests for specific individuals).

Notifications
~14 tables · Tier 4 Observational · real-time in-app and outbound alerts
When a claim has been sitting unreviewed for five days, a supervisor needs to know. When a
Direct Certification load fails overnight, the state agency DC coordinator needs to know before
caseworkers start their morning. When a sponsor's application is approved, the sponsor needs
to know. This domain manages every system-generated alert the platform produces — what
triggered it, who it was for, how it was delivered, and whether delivery succeeded.
This domain is distinct from Communications & Email. Communications & Email is for human-
authored correspondence: a state agency staff member drafting a deadline reminder, a bulk
outreach email to all SFSP sponsors. Notifications is for machine-generated alerts that fire
automatically based on workflow events, threshold breaches, and scheduled conditions. No
human composes a Notification. The platform generates it from a template when a triggering
condition is met.
NotificationTemplates defines the alert types: what event triggers the notification, which
programs it applies to, what the message says, and whether it should be delivered in-app, by
email, or both. NotificationQueue holds pending notifications before they are sent — a
decoupled write that allows the platform to continue processing even if the email gateway is
temporarily unavailable. NotificationDeliveries logs every send attempt including failures, so a
state agency can confirm a notification was actually received and retry if it was not.
UserNotificationPreferences lets individual users control which alert types they want and
through which channel, within the limits the state agency administrator has configured for their
tenant.
NotificationTemplat
es
Template for each alert type: trigger event, program scope, subject, body,
delivery channel (in-app / email / both). Lives in cnp_global — templates
are shared across all states.
NotificationQueue Pending notifications: recipient, entity reference, scheduled send time,
status. Decoupled from the triggering event so delivery failures don't
affect the operational workflow.
Table What it holds
<!-- page: 46 -->
CnpAlerts (in Workflow & Tasks) are internal system conditions — a background job detecting
that a review is overdue. Notifications is the outbound layer: CnpAlerts writes to
NotificationQueue, which then delivers the message to the user. CnpAlerts is the detection;
Notifications is the delivery.
Reference Data & Transparency
~12 tables · Tier 4 Observational · shared lookup values and public reference data
Every dropdown in the platform — program type, eligibility status, finding code, claim status,
review type — draws its values from this domain. When a form needs to present a list of valid
options, or a compliance reviewer needs to select a finding category, the list comes from here.
This is the master repository of all codes and classifications that multiple domains share, kept in
cnp_global so every state reads from the same authoritative source.
This domain also holds the reference data USDA publishes for public transparency: poverty line
percentages used in eligibility determinations, program participation thresholds, and the
canonical list of federal programs the platform supports. These values change infrequently — a
poverty line update once a year, a new program added once a decade — and when they do
change the update is a database INSERT with an effective date, not a code deployment.
LookupCodes is the single most-read table in the system. Every page load that renders a status
badge, a program type label, or a dropdown list reads from it. It lives in cnp_global and is
cached aggressively. SystemSettings holds platform-wide configuration values that don't
belong to any specific program domain and don't need the feature flag infrastructure of
LaunchDarkly — things like default page sizes, session timeout durations, and environment
identifiers.

LaunchDarkly
~8 tables · Tier 4 Observational · feature flag and session replay configuration
The platform uses LaunchDarkly as its feature management service. Whether a state has
access to the SSFO module, whether non-congregate meal service is enabled for an SFSP
tenant, whether Session Replay is capturing sessions for a specific user role — these are
controlled through LaunchDarkly flags, not code deployments. This domain is the local database
representation of that flag configuration: which flags exist, what their default values are, and
which per-tenant overrides are active.
LaunchDarkly itself is an external service. The platform does not re-implement flag evaluation —
it calls the LaunchDarkly SDK. This domain exists for two reasons. First, it provides a local cache
of flag definitions so that a LaunchDarkly service interruption does not cause the platform to
behave unpredictably — flags fall back to their last-known value. Second, it makes flag
configuration auditable through the same audit infrastructure as the rest of the platform: a
change to a tenant flag override writes to FieldChangeLog, just like a change to any other
operational record.
FeatureFlagDefinitions is the registry of all flag keys the platform uses, their type, and their
default value. It lives in cnp_global — the flag schema is the same for all states.
LookupCodes All *Types, *Codes, *Statuses used throughout the system. Category +
Code + Description + DisplayOrder. Every dropdown value, every status
badge label. Lives in cnp_global. Codes are standardized across all states
by design. State-specific display label overrides, if needed, are a separate
concern handled at the presentation layer, not additional rows here.
SystemSettings Platform-wide configuration values: session timeouts, default pagination
sizes, environment identifiers. Not tenant-specific, not feature-flagged.

nitions

TenantFlagOverrides stores the per-state exceptions: Utah has Session Replay enabled at a 10%
sample rate; Hawaii has the Training module enabled; Indiana has DirectVer enabled. Each
override row records when it was enabled and by whom. SessionReplayConfig extends
TenantFlagOverrides for the Session Replay capability specifically, capturing the sample rate,
PII masking configuration, and retention policy since these require more structured storage than
a simple boolean override.
A Closer Look at the Data
Biggest Table Collapses 
In total, roughly 840 of the 1,243 CTS tables were absorbed into roughly 25 greenfield tables.
The 413 "Keep" tables are the ones that represent distinct data concepts that couldn't be
collapsed further.
LookupCodes 353 → 1 table. The single largest collapse. CTS had one dedicated table per
code list (SiteTypes, MealTypes, SponsorTypes, FnsReportTypes, EthnicTypes, etc.). Each one of
those becomes a category of rows in a single LookupCodes  table.
Review Engine 188 → 7 tables. CTS modeled form variation structurally — one table set per
review worksheet type. Every new review instrument required new tables. Greenfield stores the
same variation as data rows, so all 188 tables fold into ReviewFormCatalog , 
ReviewQuestions , ReviewAnswerOptions , ReviewBusinessRules  (cnp_global) plus
their instance counterparts (cnp_ops).
Form Engine  99 → 10 tables. Same pattern as reviews, applied to application forms, site detail
worksheets, budget worksheets, and annual renewals. One table set per form type in CTS
becomes rows in FormDefinitions , FormSections , FormFields , etc.
FeatureFlagDefinitions Registry of all LaunchDarkly flag keys: flag key, type
(bool/string/number), default value, description, which module it
gates. Lives in cnp_global.
TenantFlagOverrides Per-state flag values that differ from the default. TenantCode +
FlagId + OverrideValue + EnabledAt + EnabledBy. Lives in cnp_ops.
SessionReplayConfig LaunchDarkly Session Replay settings per tenant: enabled flag,
sample rate (0–100%), PII field mask list, session retention period in
days.
Table What it holds
<!-- page: 49 -->
Fully eliminated 180 tables Temp tables, shuffle tables, version-tracking tables, and CTS
deployment artifacts that have no greenfield equivalent at all.
RBAC roughly 20 tables, but also + 5,000+ ACL rows → 6 tables. Not a large table count
collapse, but a significant data model collapse The ACL-per-user-per-object pattern is replaced
by role-based permissions with only tenant-level overrides where needed.
Tradeoffs/Risks
Referential integrity moves to the API layer. In CTS, SiteApplications.SiteTypeCode
can FK directly to SiteTypes.SiteTypeCode . The database enforces it. With everything
collapsed into LookupCodes , we can no longer express that constraint in DDL. The same is
true for FormFieldValues: all values stored as TEXT, cast at read time. If the API has a bug,
invalid data gets in with no database-level backstop. 
FormFieldValues and ReviewAnswers will be the largest tables in the system. Every form
instance × every field = rows. Across 5 states with heavy claim seasons, this grows fast. The
indexing strategy on those two tables needs to be designed deliberately before build, not
retrofitted when it slows down.
Reporting complexity increases significantly. Queries that were trivial in CTS ("show all sites
that answered Yes to question X") become multi-join Entity-Attribute-Value lookups. State FNS
reports often need specific field values aggregated. This isn't a blocker, but whoever writes the
reporting layer needs to know they're working against an EAV model, not typed columns. We
gain flexibility and maintainability over database-enforced structure, but queries get complex
and bad data can slip in if the API has a gap.
The RBAC collapse carries migration risk. 5,000+ ACL rows imply highly granular, per-entity
permissions that evolved organically over years. Mapping those to the new role model is where
access regressions are most likely to hide as either over-permissive (something opens up that
shouldn't) or over-restrictive (a workflow breaks). This mapping needs line-by-line verification
against actual production ACL data before cutover, and that verification has to happen onshore
since the offshore team can't see production.
The 180 eliminated tables need dependency verification. Temp and version-tracking tables
are obvious drops. The risk is stored procedures or scheduled jobs in CTS that reference them.
Since the offshore team has zero access to the existing codebase, that dependency check has
to be an explicit onshore task before anything is actually dropped.
